Autre question de terminologie : le Congrès avait adopté d'enthousiasme une belle terminologie symétrique : ``poids'', ``poids radiciels'', ``copoids'', ``copoids radiciels''. Le malheur est qu'avec la définition adoptée, un ``copoids radiciel'' \uline{n'est pas} nécessairement un ``copoids'', ce qui est grammaticalement intolérable. Le rédacteur voit trois solutions possibles :

1) Prendre une autre terminologie pour ``poids radiciels'' et ``copoids radiciels'' ; c'est la solution adoptée dans la rédaction, qui dit respectivement ``vocables'' et ``covocables'', (dactylo, attention, ce n'est \uline{pas} ``convocables''!). Le rédacteur ne tient pas spécialement à ces termes ; on pourrait aussi dire ``noeuds'' et ``conoeuds'' bien que ce dernier mot ait l'air un peu ... ce que vous pensez.

2) On ne peut naturellement changer le sens reçu de ``racines'' et ``poids'' ; mais ``copoids'' est beaucoup plus récent, (Chevalley, je crois), et pas encore très répandu ; on pourrait donc intervertir les sens de ``copoids'' et ``copoids radiciels'', les poids étant donc associés aux copoids radiciels, (et non plus aux copoids), et les copoids radiciels étant engendrés par les coracines, (ce qui est assez satisfaisant).

3) N'utiliser aucune terminologie pour ``poids radiciels'' et ``copoids radiciels'' ; l'expérience, (tout au moins dans la présente rédaction), montre qu'on s'en sert en fait très peu et qu'on s'en passe fort bien.
**Manuscript:** “un “copoids radiciel” n’est pas nécessairement un “copoids””

The three editorial alternatives are a new vocabulary (vocables/covocables), swapping the meanings of copoids and copoids radiciels, or avoiding names for the rarely used objects. The page says the first option is used in this draft, not that it became the final published convention.

The parenthetical attribution of “copoids” to Chevalley is explicitly tentative in the source. Any historical discussion should preserve that uncertainty and verify it from dated primary texts rather than convert it to a firm attribution.

The previous isomorphism argument cannot simply be applied to an injection between spaces of different dimensions, because no inverse exists on the whole target. If the correspondence algebra of the direct sum of source and target, with the required Tate twist, is semisimple, its matrix-block structure gives a generalized inverse \(g\) with \(fgf=f\), and injectivity of the realized \(f\) then yields \(gf=1\) on the source. **Kind:** unpursued implication. **Location:** cote 16, scan 49, parenthetical “category of motives which is semi-simple”.

Jannsen (1992, Theorem 1) proves, for characteristic-zero coefficient fields and adequate equivalence relations, that the category of pure motives is semisimple abelian precisely when the equivalence relation is numerical. Thus numerical motives provide a later unconditional realization of the broad semisimplicity goal, without assuming the standard conjectures. The manuscript's actual operators, however, act on a chosen cohomology theory and are taken modulo homological equivalence, so transferring the conclusion to that category requires identifying the relevant equivalence relations. Quotienting by numerical equivalence changes the problem unless that identification has been established.

### S15 — Numerical motives have a later unconditional theorem

Jannsen (1992, Theorem 1) proves, for characteristic-zero coefficient fields and adequate equivalence relations, that the category of pure motives is semisimple abelian precisely when the equivalence relation is numerical. Thus numerical motives provide a later unconditional realization of the broad semisimplicity goal, without assuming the standard conjectures. The manuscript's actual operators, however, act on a chosen cohomology theory and are taken modulo homological equivalence, so transferring the conclusion to that category requires identifying the relevant equivalence relations. Quotienting by numerical equivalence changes the problem unless that identification has been established.

Finite étale covers are indeed invariant under nilpotent thickenings, and the modern statement allows arbitrary thickenings of schemes (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BQB, Lemma 58.8.3). ### S16 — A nilpotent kernel is not a zero kernel

Under algebraicity of the Künneth components, Jannsen (1992, Corollary 1) identifies the kernel from homological to numerical degree-zero correspondence algebras with the Jacobson radical and proves it nilpotent. This isolates a precise obstruction to obtaining the draft's cohomological semisimplicity from numerical semisimplicity. Nilpotence alone permits a nonzero ideal, so it is not a proof that the two equivalence relations coincide; an additional positivity or equivalence argument must annihilate that kernel. A useful later comparison distinguishes a particular bundle’s integral Chern classes from an integral Fourier transform on the entire Chow group. Beckmann and de Gaay Fortman (2023, Theorem 3.8) characterize integral lifts of the Poincaré character using a specific one-cycle; under a symmetric ample principal polarization, they also relate this to preservation of Chow groups modulo torsion and to weak integral Fourier transforms.
